## Simple explanation

A vector is a list of numbers treated as one mathematical object. For example,
the coordinates $(2, 5)$ form a two-dimensional vector that can locate a point
or describe a direction.

## Technical explanation

An $n$-dimensional vector is an element of a vector space, often written
$x\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Vectors can be added and scaled, and their components can
represent coordinates or measured features. A vector's representation depends
on its basis; its values are not meaningful without knowing the feature order
and units.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Models represent inputs, hidden activations, gradients, and outputs as vectors.
Understanding vector dimensions and operations helps diagnose shape errors,
choose similarity measures, and interpret embeddings.

## How it works

Common operations include addition, scalar multiplication, dot product, and
norm. The dot product $x^\top y$ measures alignment in Euclidean coordinates;
the Euclidean norm $\lVert x\rVert_2$ measures magnitude. Normalizing a
nonzero vector divides it by its norm.

## Practical example

A text model may encode a sentence as a vector with hundreds of components.
The vector can be compared with another sentence vector using cosine
similarity, provided both vectors use a compatible embedding model.

## Common misconceptions

- A vector is not merely any array in code; its dimensional meaning and
  operations are part of the model's representation.
- Equal vector dimensions do not guarantee that vectors from different models
  or embedding versions are comparable.
